payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
On September 1, 2026, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest in the consolidated OpenAI copyright litigation in the Southern District of New York. A statement of interest is a filing the government may make to attend to United States interests in a pending case without becoming a party to it. The document runs twenty pages, argues that training a large language model on copyrighted text is fair use, and is docketed against all matters in the multidistrict case rather than the New York Times action alone.

It takes its account of how these models get built from the court's own earlier opinion, and holds the parts of that process apart as distinct questions of copyright law.

The stages the brief keeps apart

Collection. A developer gathers and stores a vast amount of content, including the plaintiffs' works.

Training. Copies of those works are fed through the model, which learns patterns from them and makes predictions.

Output. The model answers user queries, subject to whatever filters the developer has built.

The government argues only the middle one. That separation is the whole document. Everything it wins, it wins by keeping the stages apart.

What the brief actually attacks

The target is a theory from Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, decided in the Northern District of California in 2025. The authors there lost, and the opinion floated an indirect substitution theory, market dilution, where outputs with the potential to flood a market with competing works would mean developers generally have to pay for training material whether or not any output resembled any particular book. The government calls that application of the fourth fair use factor deeply flawed, and says the court collapsed training and outputs into a single continuous use.

The stated reason repays a close reading. Market dilution, the brief argues, overlooks the most basic element of infringement, which is whether two works are substantially similar. Competition at the level of a genre does not count, since a genre is not copyrightable in the first place. What the government asks for instead is the use-by-use analysis the Supreme Court described in Warhol v. Goldsmith, one challenged use at a time, decided on its own facts.

An argument about inference

Set aside who benefits. Market dilution reasons from a population to an instance, observing the volume of synthetic work now competing for the same audience and concluding something about one act performed on one catalog. Detection reasons in that same direction, deriving a score from how a corpus behaves and applying it to a file, which is why the difference between a score and a signature keeps deciding what a record is worth in a dispute. The brief's own illustration is Joan Didion typing out Hemingway stories to learn how the sentences worked. Under the theory it attacks, she owed him every time she published.

What a use-by-use test needs

Every question the filing leaves open is about a specific artifact. One is whether a particular file was lawfully obtained. Another asks if a given output is substantially similar to a given work, and the brief concedes that one directly: at the output stage, a model that reconstructs and disseminates an original may not be transformative at all. Evidence for that kind of claim has to be found inside a model, and that evidence is engineered out of the next checkpoint. Evidence about how a file was obtained sits in a record made at the time, or it sits nowhere.

The brief cites Bartz v. Anthropic approvingly, for training being transformative. That is the same case Anthropic settled with a class of authors for $1.5 billion.

The complaint thirty-five music publishers filed against Anthropic on August 28 is already built along those lines. It separates torrenting from scraping, training and outputs, and adds a fourth count that never touches fair use, over the removal of the ownership data attached to a work, at up to $25,000 an instance. However the training question resolves, that count asks only whether such data was stripped from a particular file. Whether removal is an injury on its own terms, separate from any copying, is the question the fair use fight leaves untouched.

References

United States. "Statement of Interest of the United States." In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, No. 25-md-3143 (S.D.N.Y.), September 1, 2026. courtlistener.com

Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 788 F. Supp. 3d 1026 (N.D. Cal. 2025).

Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508 (2023).

Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, 787 F. Supp. 3d 1007 (N.D. Cal. 2025).

Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell Music, et al. v. Anthropic PBC. Complaint, N.D. Cal., filed August 28, 2026.
